messages.content: You are a helpful assistant experienced in coworking and small-business operations, helping a founder open a second location of their coworking space.

Hey, so Loomworks is opening its second location, this time in a converted warehouse across the city, and it's a way bigger job than our first spot. I want to use you as a planning partner across buildout, pricing, staffing, software, marketing, all of it. Cool?
Sounds great — let's work through buildout, pricing, staffing, software, and marketing one at a time, starting with the floor plan.

Let's start with the floor plan since it locks in everything else. It's a big open warehouse shell. How should I think about balancing open desks, private offices, and meeting rooms for a second location?
Think about your first location's usage data, how much recurring private-office demand you actually have versus walk-in desk demand, and leave room to convert space later as the mix becomes clearer.
On pricing, we're deciding between keeping the same tiers as our first location or introducing a cheaper part-time tier for the new spot. What's the general tradeoff?
A cheaper part-time tier can widen your funnel in a new neighborhood, but weigh whether it cannibalizes full members or just adds incremental revenue.

Quick clarification: when I say 'the floor' to you, I always mean the open coworking desk area specifically, not the entire building or the physical flooring material, even though the contractors keep saying 'the floor' to mean the concrete slab. Just the open desk area, when I say it to you.
Understood, I'll keep that scoped correctly going forward.
For staffing, is it better to transfer an experienced community manager from the first location or hire someone new who knows the neighborhood?
Transferring an experienced manager preserves your culture and playbook faster, while a local hire brings neighborhood relationships you'd otherwise have to build from scratch.

Floor plan decision time. We looked at three layouts: (1) mostly open desks with just a few private offices, (2) mostly private offices with a small open area, or (3) a hybrid with a central open core ringed by private offices and meeting rooms on the perimeter. After talking with our designer, we're going with the hybrid, open core ringed by private offices.
That's a smart way to balance flexibility with a sense of openness in the space.
On software, our current access-and-booking system is clunky. What features matter most when a coworking space shops for a new one?
Look for solid door-hardware integration, flexible booking rules, and reliable billing — those tend to matter more day to day than flashy extras.

Hard preference on pricing: absolutely no long-term lock-in contracts for members. I think forcing people into annual commitments is exactly the landlord-y behavior our whole brand rejects. I don't care how much it would smooth our revenue, memberships stay month-to-month, always.
Understood, I'll keep that boundary in mind for anything pricing-related.

Also, when I say 'the hub' from now on, I mean the staffed front reception-and-community desk, not our members-only mobile app which the team also nicknamed 'the hub.' Two different things, and I only mean the physical reception desk.
Got it, noted the distinction.
For the buildout, how much should I budget for soundproofing the phone booths and meeting rooms specifically?
Budget generously for phone booths and meeting rooms specifically; noise complaints are one of the most common member frustrations in open warehouse spaces.

For context, we used a printing-and-signage vendor called Copperline Print for our first location's launch and they missed the deadline by two weeks and printed our logo in the wrong color. We will never use Copperline Print again.
Noted, I'll steer clear of that vendor in anything I suggest.

On the access software, we had three options on the table: (1) Kisi for door access paired with a separate booking tool, (2) an all-in-one platform called Nexudus, or (3) building a lightweight custom system on top of our existing hardware. We talked it through and we're going with Nexudus, the all-in-one platform.
Makes sense given the convenience of having everything in one platform.
Back to pricing, how many membership tiers is too many before it just confuses people?
Three or four tiers is usually the ceiling before prospective members start feeling decision fatigue; simpler is almost always better.
Random note for the file: the warehouse lease base rent is $14,200 a month before the escalation clause kicks in. Just logging that, doesn't change what we're discussing.
Logged, thanks for the note.

One more firm rule: no selling members' contact data or email lists to sponsors or partners, ever. A space I used to work at did that and it destroyed the trust of the whole community. Members' data stays private, full stop, even if a sponsor waves money at us.
Got it, noted — that'll shape how we think about sponsorship deals going forward.
For staffing, what's a sane ratio of community staff to members at a location our size?
One community staffer per roughly 60-80 members tends to keep the vibe personal without overstaffing.
Let's just codename the whole second-location launch 'Snorlax' from here on, in every planning doc and email, so we're not spelling it out every time.
Works for me — I'll use that name going forward.

Also, remember we tried a coffee supplier called Marrow Roasters at the first location and members constantly complained the beans were stale and the delivery was unreliable. We dropped them and aren't going back.
Understood, that supplier's off the table.
On marketing, what's the most effective channel for filling a new coworking space before opening day?
Local business associations, targeted social ads, and partnering with nearby cafes or gyms tend to outperform broad awareness campaigns pre-opening.
For the record, our commercial occupancy permit application is filed under number OCC-2026-58317, submitted May 12th, with the city quoting six to eight weeks. Just logging it.
Got it, thanks for flagging.
For the floor plan, how much of the square footage should stay as flexible event space versus fixed desks?
Somewhere around 15-20% flexible event space gives you upside for revenue and community programming without eating too far into stable desk revenue.
Let's codename the soundproofing and acoustics work 'Charizard', since it's the most expensive and behind-schedule part of the whole buildout. Use that name for it in any status update.
Sounds good, I'll refer to it that way in updates.
On software, how important is it that the access system integrates with the door hardware we already own?
Quite important — ripping out door hardware you already own adds cost and installation time you don't need for a launch timeline.
For the launch, how far ahead should we start pre-selling founding memberships?
Start pre-selling founding memberships two to three months out, once the space is far enough along that people can picture it.
One more on marketing: should we run the launch event before or after we've onboarded the first wave of members?
Run the launch event after the first wave has settled in, so there's real energy and testimonials to show off, not just an empty room.
How many desks can we realistically fit on the floor without it feeling cramped?
Realistically somewhere in the 60-80 desk range before it starts feeling tight, depending on aisle width and how many are dedicated versus hot desks.
Should the hub be staffed during evening hours at the new location?
Yes, staffing it into the evening helps with member retention, at least on the busiest weeknights even if not every night.
On the layout decision, no need to walk through it again, but what lighting plan does it call for?
Plan for layered lighting — brighter overhead in the open core, warmer and more adjustable in the private offices and meeting rooms.
For the software we picked, don't re-explain what it is, just tell me what the onboarding import needs from us first.
They'll need your member roster, current booking rules, and door-hardware specs to get the import started.
What's still open on the Snorlax punch list before we can set an opening date?
Mainly finalizing the founding-member pricing sheet and the staffing plan — both are close but not signed off yet.
Any movement on Charizard this week, or is the acoustics work still stuck?
Still stuck — the acoustic panels are backordered, so no real progress since last week.
For staffing, how should we structure the hiring so we're not just poaching our own first location dry?
Post the new role broadly and set a clear no-poach norm with current managers, so you're not just draining your first location's bench.
